event: Elsie wakes to the bread smell, with Tamsin's knuckle wrap on the sill beside Sunny.
prose: Elsie woke to the bread smell and lay still for a moment, listening to the ovens knock below, before she remembered why her chest felt so full. Then she turned her head on the pillow. Tamsin's knuckle wrap lay on the sill where she had put it last night, smoothed flat, beside Sunny's pot, with the grey dawn light coming through the round window onto it. It was faintly stained with blue from the moonbells. The carnation in its cup had dropped another petal onto it in the night. Elsie lay and looked at the two of them together.

event: Through the Tether she feels Tamsin somewhere across town: a sore, warm ache in one forearm.
prose: Then she felt it. It was very faint, and she had to lie quite still to be sure of it: a thread running out from under her breastbone, warm, out through the round window and away across the roofs, somewhere toward the docks. And at the far end of it, an ache. A sore, warm, dull ache in a forearm, just below the elbow, on the inside, as if someone had slept on a bruise. It was not her arm. Elsie touched her own forearm anyway, and smiled at the ceiling. Tamsin was awake, then, somewhere across town, and her arm hurt, but only a little.

memory.fact: Elsie can feel when someone bound to her is hurting.

event: She opens her window by wishing and reads the new word under Tether: Hold.
prose:
She sat up with the blanket round her shoulders and wished her window open, there in the grey light.

:::status-assessment
name: Elsie Fairweather
level: 2
note: Experience: 30 / 150; Skills: Captivate, Tether — Tamsin, Hold; Bonds: Tamsin 65, Tilly 50, Cora 10
:::

She read it all through, slowly, and then went back to the new word under Tether and stopped there. Hold. It had come to her on the apothecary's step last night with Tilly reading over her shoulder, and she had been too tired to think about it. She thought about it now, with her knees drawn up under the blanket.

memory.fact: At level 2 Elsie gains the Enthraller skill Hold.

event: She says it aloud twice, once like a gaoler and once like a hug, and settles on the hug.
prose: "Hold," she said out loud, to the attic. She said it the way a gaoler would say it, low and hard, with a hand on the bars: Hold. It sounded horrible. It sounded like the inside of a cell. She tried it again, softly, the way a person says it to someone crying, with her arms already going round them: hold. Hold on. I've got you. That was better. That was much better. "Hold," Elsie said a third time, the soft way, and nodded to herself, decided. She would think of it like that, and if anyone asked her, that was what it meant.

event: She waters the plants and tells Mrs Pennywhistle the fern that she has levelled up.
prose: She filled the jug and watered the plants one at a time along the crate, and came to Mrs Pennywhistle first, because she was oldest and ought to hear important news before the others. "I've levelled up," Elsie told the fern in a whisper, tipping the water round her roots. "Last night. On a doorstep, in the middle of the night, in front of an apothecary in a nightcap. I'm level two." The fern's long fronds trembled in the draught from the window. "I know," Elsie said, very pleased. "I didn't think it would happen so soon either."

event: Downstairs the baker sets out a honey bun for her unasked, and Elsie pays for it.
prose: Downstairs the bakery was all heat and the first trays, and the baker was sliding loaves onto the racks. When she saw Elsie on the stairs she kept quiet, but took a honey bun off the nearest tray, still glossy and steaming, and set it on the counter at Elsie's place in a twist of paper. Elsie had not asked for it. She smiled, and opened her purse, and found only silver in it; so she laid a lantern on the counter. The baker looked at it, and counted nine pips back into her palm without a word.

changes.note: One pip for the honey bun the baker set out: 110 → 109 pips

event: Elsie asks if the honey cake in the window has a recipe; the baker says it lives in her hands.
prose: Elsie ate the bun standing at the counter, and looked past the baker at the window where the honey cake sat. It sat there every day on its glass stand, round and dark gold and glistening, and people stopped on the canal path to look at it. "Is there a recipe for that?" Elsie asked. "The honey cake. Is it written down somewhere?" The baker paused with a loaf in each hand and followed her look to the window. "It lives in my hands," she said, and held them up, floury and broad, as if that were an answer. Then she racked the loaves.

event: Elsie says Tamsin's mother loves honey cake, and asks if she might learn it one day.
prose: "Tamsin's mother loves honey cake," Elsie said. "Tamsin's my friend. The one with the axe, who walked me home last night. Her mother runs a barge on the Long Cut, and she loves honey cake, Tamsin said so, and I want to bring her one when I meet her." She licked honey off her thumb and looked at the baker hopefully. "Do you think I might learn it? One day? Not now, I know you're busy. Only if you'd let me. I'd pay for everything. I'd wash up." She stopped, because the baker had put down the loaves.

memory.fact: Tamsin grew up on a canal barge, and her mother still runs it on the Long Cut.
Tamsin's mother likes honey cake.

event: The baker looks at her a long moment and says: tonight, after closing, bring the firewood money.
prose: The baker looked at her. She looked for a long moment across the counter, with her floury hands resting on the wood and her round face very still, the way she had looked at Elsie the morning Elsie had said Enthraller. It went on so long that Elsie began to be sorry she had asked. Then the baker said, "Tonight. After closing." She turned back to her ovens. "Bring the firewood money," she said over her shoulder. And she pulled out a tray with a clang, and that was all, and Elsie stood at the counter with her mouth open and the paper of the bun in her hand.

event: At the guild hall heads turn as Elsie comes in, and the talk drops to whispers.
prose: The guild hall was loud at a quarter past eight, as it was every morning. Elsie came in out of Brightwater Square with her satchel and her clip in, and for a moment it stayed loud. Then it was not. Heads turned. All along the long tables and down the length of the board, heads turned to look at her as she came in, and the talk dropped. It did not stop. It sank, all at once, to a low rustling murmur, whispers behind hands, and under it Elsie could hear her own boots on the boards. She smiled at the nearest table. They looked away.

event: Two swordsmen at the board say Enthraller, and Tether, and Berserker, and stare at her.
prose: She went to the quest board as she did each morning and stood in front of the F-rank notices. Two swordsmen were standing a little way along, young men in mail, with their heads together. Elsie did not mean to listen, but they were not quiet about it. "Enthraller," one said. "That's her." And the other, low: "Tether. On the Berserker. Reyes. In the Glasswood, in her Frenzy, my cousin had it from the gate clerk." "She turned her?" "Turned her round. Like a dog on a lead." They were both staring at Elsie now, openly. She looked back at them.

memory.fact: By morning the guild hall has heard that an Enthraller's Tether turned a Berserker in her Frenzy.
By morning the guild hall has heard that an Enthraller's Tether turned a Berserker in her Frenzy.

event: Tamsin shoulders through the door with her forearm bandaged, and grins at Elsie across the hall.
prose: The doors banged open behind her, and Tamsin shouldered through them with Margery over one shoulder and her other forearm bandaged white from wrist to elbow, held a little across her body. Every head that had turned for Elsie turned for Tamsin. Tamsin did not seem to notice them. She looked across the hall, over all those heads, straight to the quest board, and found Elsie, and grinned at her: the whole crooked grin, wide and sudden and bright, bright as a struck match. Elsie felt the thread under her breastbone go warm.

event: Elsie checks the bandage at once, and Tamsin lets her, standing very still.
prose: Elsie was across the hall to her before she had decided to go. "Let me see," she said, and took Tamsin's bandaged arm in both hands and turned it to the light from the high windows, there in the middle of the floor with everyone watching. She pressed gently round the bandage with her fingertips, feeling for heat and swelling. Tamsin let her. She stood quite still, Margery on her shoulder, with her arm held out in Elsie's hands and her green eyes on Elsie's bent head, and did not seem to breathe much. The bandage was clean and dry. There was no heat.

event: Tamsin says she slept the whole night through, the first time in a year, and can't say why.
prose: "It's good," Elsie said, satisfied, and looked up. Tamsin was still looking at her. "I slept," Tamsin said. She said it as if it were strange news from a long way off. "Last night. The whole night through, from when I lay down till the gulls. Didn't wake once." She shook her head slowly. "I haven't done that in a year. More. I wake up three, four times a night, always have, since the first time I—" She stopped. "But I slept. Like a stone. And I can't say why." She looked at Elsie a moment longer, frowning a little.

memory.fact: The night after the Tether, Tamsin slept the night through for the first time in a year.
The night after the Tether, Tamsin slept the night through for the first time in a year.
The night after the Tether, Tamsin slept the night through for the first time in a year.
The night after the Tether, Tamsin slept the night through for the first time in a year.

event: Tilly arrives at a run with a pear fizz for each of them, and they drink them at the board.
prose: Running boots, and clinking, and Tilly came through the doors at a run with three tall stoppered bottles held against her chest in both arms, each one full of something pale gold and fizzing. Her goggles were up and her braids were flying and there was a fresh smear of soot across her cheek. "Pear fizz," she panted, skidding to a stop. "For waking up. One each. I made them last night, I couldn't sleep." She pressed one on Elsie and one on Tamsin, and they unstoppered them there at the quest board and drank, and the fizz went up Elsie's nose and she laughed and sneezed.

event: Elsie wipes soot off Tilly's cheek with her thumb, and Tilly forgets what she was saying.
prose: Tilly was talking, fast and bright, about how she had got the fizz to taste properly of pear at last by adding the pear later, and waving her bottle. The soot on her cheek was a big dark smudge. Elsie reached out without thinking and cupped Tilly's jaw in her hand and wiped it off with her thumb, slowly, from her cheekbone to the corner of her mouth. Tilly stopped. She stopped mid-word with her mouth still open on it, and her blue eyes went wide and fixed on Elsie's, and she went pink. "And then—" she said. "And then. I. What was I saying?"

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 50 → 55 (Elsie wiped the soot off her cheek)

event: Cora comes out of the charcoal door and says the guildmaster wants Elsie upstairs, with Tamsin.
prose: The charcoal-painted door opened across the hall, and Cora came out, with the ledger under her arm, and came straight through the crowd to them. The whispering parted for her coat. She stopped in her place, a step behind Elsie, and inclined her head. "Fairweather," she said. "The guildmaster wants you upstairs. Now, before the hall's business starts." Her grey eyes went to Tamsin's bandaged arm, and back. "With Reyes," she said. Tamsin's grin went a little crooked. Tilly looked from one of them to the other with her bottle clutched to her chest.

event: Elsie buys Cora a black tea with one sugar at the hall counter and hands it to her.
prose: "Just a moment," Elsie said, and went to the hall counter by the stairs, where a woman sold tea in thick white cups to adventurers waiting on the board. "One black tea, please," Elsie said. "Strong. One sugar." She counted two copper pips out of her purse onto the counter, and watched the woman drop the sugar in and stir it, and took the cup in both hands, careful, and carried it back through the crowd to Cora without spilling a drop. She held it out to her. "For the stairs," she said. "You'll want it. It's a long way up."

changes.note: Two pips for Cora's black tea, one sugar, at the hall counter: 109 → 107 pips

memory.fact: Cora drinks her tea black and strong with one sugar.

event: Cora takes it without a word, and drinks it on the stairs.
prose: Cora looked at the cup. She looked at it, steaming, in Elsie's hands, and then at Elsie, a short grey look. Then she took it without a word, holding it by the body rather than the handle, the way a person holds a cup to warm her fingers, though the morning was warm. And on the way up the stairs to the guildmaster's office, climbing a step ahead of Elsie and Tamsin, Elsie saw her lift it and drink, and drink again, and by the top of the stairs the cup was empty, and Cora was holding it carefully, as if she did not know where to put it down.

changes.note: Bond: Cora 10 → 15 (Elsie bought her tea as she takes it; Cora drank it)

event: Tilly waits by the board while Elsie, Tamsin and Cora go up to the guildmaster's office.
prose: Tilly did not come up. The guildmaster had asked for Elsie and Tamsin, and Tilly stood at the foot of the stairs with her fizz bottle and her face anxious, and said she would wait by the board, she didn't mind, she'd wait right there, and went. Elsie looked back at her from halfway up and waved, and Tilly waved her bottle. Then they went on up, Cora first with her empty cup, then Elsie, then Tamsin, heavy-footed on the narrow stairs, and along a short passage to a door at the end, and Cora knocked.

event: The guildmaster has grey hair and a sword on the wall, and asks Cora for the ledger.
prose: The guildmaster's office was a plain room with a big window over the square and a desk heaped with papers. The guildmaster sat behind it: grey-haired, broad in the shoulder, in her fifties, with a face like weathered oak and a swordswoman's straight back, and on the wall behind her, on two pegs, hung a long sword in a plain worn scabbard. She looked at the three of them as they came in. Then she held out her hand across the desk, palm up, to Cora. "The ledger, Warden," she said. Cora set down her cup and gave it to her.

memory.fact: The guildmaster is a grey-haired retired A-rank swordswoman in her fifties, with an office upstairs.

event: She reads the Glasswood page and asks Tamsin if she gave her leave.
prose: The guildmaster opened it and turned the pages until she found the one she wanted, and read it. She read it slowly, with one finger moving down the lines, and her face stayed closed. Elsie stood in front of the desk with her hands folded and waited. The room was very quiet. Then the guildmaster looked up from the page, not at Elsie, but past her at Tamsin. "Reyes," she said. "It says here you gave the Enthraller leave to use her Tether on you. Before the guild. Did you give it?"

memory.fact: An Enthraller's Warden writes down every skill she uses and reports it to the guildmaster.
An Enthraller's Warden writes down every skill she uses and reports it to the guildmaster.

event: Tamsin says yes, before the guild, and she would give it again right now.
prose: "Yes," Tamsin said at once. She said it loud, the way she had said it at the quest board, with her chin up and her bandaged arm held across her. "I gave it. In the hall, in front of the Warden, out loud, and she wrote it down. That's my leave." She glanced at Elsie, and back at the guildmaster, and her ears went pink. "And I'd give it again. Right now. Right here, in front of you, if you want to hear it twice." She squared her shoulders. "I'll give it every day if that's what it takes."

event: The guildmaster asks Elsie what the Tether does, and Elsie tells her plainly, the ache too.
prose: The guildmaster nodded slowly and turned her eyes to Elsie. "Fairweather," she said. "Tell me what it does. Your Tether. In your own words, not the Warden's." Elsie told her. She told it plainly, because that was how she spoke: the warmth leaving her chest, the thread of light, gold and thin as a hair, running from her to Tamsin; Tamsin's eyes finding her through the red; Tamsin turning her back and fighting only the wolves. "And I can feel her," Elsie said. "When she's hurt. Her arm aches in my arm. It ached this morning. I knew where the bite was before I saw it."

memory.fact: Elsie can feel when someone bound to her is hurting.
Elsie can feel when someone bound to her is hurting.

event: Elsie says Tamsin may break it whenever she likes; Tamsin says she likes it where it is.
prose: "And she can break it," Elsie said quickly. "Whenever she likes. That's what it is, a pact; the one bound can break it any time, she only has to want to. I told her so before, and I told her again after, in the wood." She turned to Tamsin. "You can. You know you can." Tamsin was looking at the sword on the wall rather than at either of them, and her ears had gone from pink to red. "I know," she said gruffly. "I like it where it is." She folded her arms, carefully, over the bandage. "So it stays."

memory.fact: A Tether Elsie makes is a pact the bound one can break at will.
A Tether Elsie makes is a pact the bound one can break at will.

event: The guildmaster says the Tether stands, and Cora goes on writing every line.
prose: The guildmaster looked from one of them to the other for a long moment. Then she closed the ledger and laid her hand flat on it. "The Tether stands," she said. "By leave given and by leave kept. It is lawful under the Accord, and I'll say so to anyone who asks me." She handed the ledger back across the desk to Cora. Cora took it, and opened it at once, there on her palm, and began to write, and she went on writing while the guildmaster spoke, every line, the pen moving small and steady down the page without a pause.

memory.fact: The guildmaster ruled Elsie's Tether on Tamsin lawful under the Accord.
The guildmaster ruled Elsie's Tether on Tamsin lawful under the Accord.
The guildmaster ruled Elsie's Tether on Tamsin lawful under the Accord.
The guildmaster ruled Elsie's Tether on Tamsin lawful under the Accord.
The guildmaster ruled Elsie's Tether on Tamsin lawful under the Accord.

event: She asks if Elsie knows what the city will say; Elsie says she hopes it says Tamsin is safe.
prose: "Do you know what the city will say, Fairweather?" the guildmaster asked. She leaned back in her chair and looked at Elsie from under her grey brows, not unkindly. "By tonight it'll be in every tavern on the canal. An Enthraller has a Berserker on a string. You'll hear it said that way. Worse ways, too." Elsie thought about it. She thought about the two swordsmen at the board, and the heads turning. "I hope," she said slowly, "it says Tamsin is safe now. And everyone near her is safe. That's what happened. I hope that's what it says."

event: Back downstairs Tilly waits by the Leftovers, and so do three of the Copper Hounds.
prose: When they came back down the stairs, Tilly was waiting where she had said, but not by the quest board; she had drifted to the Leftovers corner, at the bottom of the party board, and was standing very straight there with her fizz bottle clutched in both hands. And she was not alone. Three adventurers stood near her in a loose knot by the slates, in good leather and copper-studded jerkins, two women and a man, with a copper hound worked on each of their shoulders. Elsie knew the slate behind them. The Copper Hounds. Tamsin, beside her, had gone quite still.

event: Their leader says the Hounds will take Tamsin back, now that she is on a leash.
prose: The tallest of the three was a broad dark-haired woman with a scar through one eyebrow, and she stepped forward as they came up, looking past Elsie at Tamsin. She did not look angry. She looked like a woman at a market who has decided she wants something after all. "Reyes," she said. "Heard about the Glasswood. Heard all about it." She jerked her head at the slate. "The Hounds'll take you back. Shield-bearer's arm's mending, and we're a hand short." Her eyes went to Elsie, and down to Elsie's chest, as if she could see the thread there. "Now that you're on a leash."

event: Tamsin's grin goes; Elsie steps in front of her before she can answer.
prose: Tamsin's grin went. Elsie saw it go out of her face all at once, the way the light had gone out of her eyes in the cellar, and something else came into it, hot and dark and ashamed, and her hands closed into fists at her sides, the bandaged one too. She opened her mouth. Elsie stepped in front of her. She did not think about it; she stepped across, quick, and stood between Tamsin and the Hound's leader with her back to Tamsin and her chin up, small and slight in her halter and skirt, and looked up into the scarred woman's face.

event: Elsie says it is no leash, it is Tamsin's, and Tamsin chooses.
prose: "It's not a leash," Elsie said. Her voice came out clear and steady, and carried, and the whispering round the board stopped to hear it. "It's not mine. It's Tamsin's." She did not know how else to say it, so she said it again, plainly. "It's a pact, and it's hers. She holds the end of it, not me. She can let go of it any time she likes. And she chooses. She chooses whether it stays, and she chooses where she goes, and who with." She looked straight at the woman. "It's hers. She chooses."

event: Tamsin puts a hand on Elsie's shoulder and says her name is chalked on a slate already.
prose: A hand came down on Elsie's shoulder from behind, warm and heavy and wrapped across the knuckles. Tamsin's hand. It rested there on Elsie's bare shoulder beside the halter tie, and Elsie felt the calluses on the palm, and the warmth, and the slight tremble in it. "My name's chalked on a slate already," Tamsin said, over Elsie's head, to the scarred woman. Her voice was quiet and very steady. She nodded at the board behind the Hounds, at the slate under theirs with three names on it in three hands. "That one. See it? Mine's the middle one."

memory.fact: Elsie, Tamsin and Tilly chalked their names on the last Leftovers slate as one party.

event: The Hounds' leader looks at Elsie a long while and goes back to her table.
prose: The leader of the Copper Hounds looked at the slate. Then she looked down at Elsie. She looked at her for a long time, a hard, measuring, puzzled look, at Elsie's face and her clip and her small hands and the tag at her belt, as if Elsie were a sum that would not come out. Elsie looked back at her and waited, and smiled a little, because she did not know what else to do with her face. Then the woman turned away without a word, and the other two followed her, and they went back to their table by the wall and sat down.

event: Tamsin keeps her hand on Elsie's shoulder the whole length of the board.
prose: Tamsin did not take her hand off Elsie's shoulder. Elsie turned toward the quest board, and Tamsin turned with her, and her hand stayed where it was, warm on Elsie's bare skin, and they walked like that the whole length of the party board and on along the quest board to the F-ranks, past every table, past the Hounds, with everyone watching. Tamsin did not say anything. Her thumb moved once on Elsie's shoulder, a small stroke, and was still. Elsie reached up and patted her hand, and left her own hand over it a while.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 65 → 75 (Elsie stood between her and the Hounds)

event: New notices are up on the F-rank board: a lost cat, a flower cart escort, glowcaps underground.
prose: There were new notices up on the F-rank board, pinned over the old ones in a fresh clean row. Elsie read them aloud for the others, one by one. "Lost cat, on the rooftops of Tanner's Row. Two lanterns." She moved her finger along. "Escort a flower cart round the lake villages. Five lanterns. That sounds lovely." And the last one, in a dyer's crabbed hand, with a little brown mushroom drawn in the corner: "Glowcaps, gathered from the Underbloom, for a dyer. Four lanterns." Tamsin leaned in to read it over her shoulder, and Tilly leaned in too, and went quiet.

event: Tilly says glowcaps mean underground, very quietly, and Elsie squeezes her hand.
prose: "Glowcaps," Tilly said, very quietly, to the notice. She was not asking. "That means underground. They only grow underground." She said it in a small flat voice, as if reading it off a label, and her hand had gone to the vials at her belt. She did not say anything else. Elsie looked at her face, and then she reached down without looking and found Tilly's other hand, hanging at her side, and took it and squeezed it, once, firmly. Tilly's fingers closed round hers and held on. Neither of them said anything about it.

event: Elsie picks the lost cat on the rooftops of Tanner's Row; Tamsin says she can climb anything.
prose: "The cat," Elsie said, decided, and tapped the notice. "Let's do the cat. Tanner's Row. Some poor old cat stuck up on a roof, and someone missing him." She looked round at them. "The cart can wait for another day, and we're not doing the glowcaps." She did not look at Tilly as she said it, and she felt Tilly's hand go soft in hers. Tamsin grinned and flexed her good arm. "Rooftops," she said. "I can climb anything. Drainpipes, chimneys, the mast of a barge in a gale. I'll have your cat down in five minutes."

event: The clerk enters the party for the cat, and Cora writes it in her ledger.
prose: They took the notice to the long desk, and the clerk entered the party for the lost cat, Fairweather and three names, and stamped it, and slid it back. Elsie turned round, and Cora was there in her place a step behind, as Elsie had known she would be, with the black ledger already open on her palm. She was writing it in: the date, the notice, the names. Her pen moved small and exact. "A cat," Elsie told her happily. Cora did not look up from the page. "A cat," she said, and wrote it down.

event: Tanner's Row smells of leather, and its roofs lean close across a narrow lane.
prose: Tanner's Row was a long, narrow, crooked lane in the old part of the city behind the tanneries, and it smelled of leather: of hides and oak bark and something sour underneath. The houses on either side were tall and old and leaned toward each other across the lane as they went up, storey on storey, until their roofs nearly touched overhead, with only a crooked strip of blue sky between them. Washing hung across from window to window. Elsie stood in the lane and tipped her head back, shading her eyes, and looked up at the roofs.

event: An old woman in a doorway says the cat is Pudding, ginger, and he will not come down.
prose: An old woman stood in a doorway halfway along, in a shawl, with her hands knotted together under her chin. When she saw Tamsin's axe and the tag at Elsie's belt she came out at once. "You're for Pudding," she said. "Oh, thank goodness." She pointed up, with a shaking finger, at the roofs. "He's ginger. Big ginger tom, with a white bib and one torn ear, you can't miss him. And he won't come down." Her voice wobbled. "I've called and called. I've put out fish. He looks at me and he won't come down."

event: She says Pudding has been up there two days and hisses at the ladder man.
prose: "Two days he's been up there," the old woman said. "Two days and two nights, in the heat and the dew, and only gutter water to drink." She dabbed her eyes with the corner of her shawl. "My neighbour's boy fetched the ladder man yesterday, and he went up, and Pudding hissed at him. Hissed and spat and swore at him like a sailor, and went up higher. The ladder man said he'd not go near him again for any money." She looked at them all, beseeching. "He's not a bad cat. He's only frightened."

event: Tamsin goes up a drainpipe to the first roof, and Pudding watches her from a chimney.
prose: Tamsin handed Margery to Elsie to hold, and the axe was so heavy that Elsie had to lean it against the wall before she dropped it. Then Tamsin spat on her hands and went up a drainpipe. She went up it like a squirrel, bandaged arm and all, hand over hand, her boots finding holds in the old brick, and swung herself over the gutter onto the first roof. She stood up on the slates. On the chimney stack at the top of that roof, a large ginger cat sat with his tail wrapped round his feet, watching her come with round yellow eyes.

event: Pudding spits at Tamsin and climbs to the next roof up.
prose: Tamsin started up the slope of the roof toward him, crouched, one hand held out. "Here, puss," she said. "Pudding. Good lad. Here." Pudding watched her come. When she was almost at the chimney, he stood up, very slowly, and arched his back, and spat at her. It was a loud, wet, furious spit, with his ears flat and every hair on end. Then he turned and leapt off the chimney onto the next roof up, across the gap, and climbed its slope to the very ridge, and sat down there with his back to her. Tamsin swore at him. Below, Tilly giggled.

event: Tilly mixes a fishy paste in her palm, apologising for the smell the whole time.
prose: "I can make something," Tilly said. "For him. Something he'll want." She sat down on the doorstep, unstoppered two vials from her belt and a little paper twist from her apron pocket, and tipped and mixed them in the cup of her palm, stirring with her finger. A smell came up. It was a strong, rank, oily smell of fish, of a great deal of fish left in the sun, and Elsie's eyes watered. "I'm sorry," Tilly said, stirring. "I'm so sorry. It's the smell. It has to smell. That's the point. Cats like it. I'm sorry. I'm sorry about the smell."

changes.note: Tilly experience 130 → 140 (judged: Brew, a fish paste for the cat)

event: Elsie climbs the ladder with the paste on a rag, and Tamsin hauls her up by both wrists.
prose: Elsie took a clean rag from her satchel and Tilly scraped the paste onto it, and Elsie folded it in half and tucked it into her belt. The ladder man's ladder was still propped against the house wall, the old woman said. Elsie climbed it. It was a long ladder, and it creaked, and it bowed a little in the middle, and the lane got very small below her. At the top the gutter was a step too high. Tamsin was there on the roof, flat on her stomach on the slates, reaching down with both hands. She caught Elsie by both wrists and hauled her up and over.

event: On the roof Tamsin keeps hold of her wrists a while, and says the slates are slippery.
prose: They landed in a heap on the warm slates. Elsie laughed, breathless, and sat up. Tamsin had not let go of her wrists. She sat on the slates facing Elsie with Elsie's wrists still held in her hands, one in each, her fingers wrapped right round them, and she did not let go. The sun was hot on the roof. Tamsin's face was flushed and her curls were full of brick dust. "Slates are slippery," Tamsin said. Her voice was a little rough. "You hold on to me. Up here. Till you've got your feet." Elsie nodded, and held on to her.

pictured.coverAfter: They landed in a heap on the warm slates. Elsie laughed, breathless, and sat

event: Cora calls up from the lane that she is staying where the ground is, and watches.
prose: "Cora!" Elsie called down over the gutter. "Are you coming up?" Far below in the lane, a small straight figure in a charcoal coat stood with the black ledger open on her palm, looking up at them with her hand shading her eyes. "No," Cora called back, in her flat clear voice, which carried up the walls perfectly well. "I am staying where the ground is." She did not move. She stood in the middle of the lane, a little apart from the old woman and Tilly, and watched them, with her head tipped back and her pen ready, and did not take her eyes off the roof.

event: Pudding sits on the ridge and looks at Elsie with flat yellow eyes.
prose: They went up the slope of the roof together on hands and knees, Tamsin first, and over the ridge and down a little and up the next, to where Pudding sat. He was on the very ridge of the highest roof in the row, with the whole tilted city spread out round him, and he had turned round to face them. He sat with his tail tucked round him and his torn ear back, and he looked at Elsie. It was a long, flat, yellow look, with no welcome in it at all, the look of a cat who has had two very bad days and blames everyone.

event: Tamsin asks if Elsie hasn't got some skill that could charm him down.
prose: Tamsin crouched on the slates beside Elsie, holding the ridge, and looked at the cat, and the cat looked at Tamsin, and Tamsin's eyes narrowed. "Haven't you got something?" she said in a low voice, out of the corner of her mouth. "A skill. Your Captivate, or your new one. Couldn't you just—" she waggled her fingers at the cat, "—charm him down? One go. He'd come right to you. Then we're done and off this roof." She looked at Elsie hopefully. "Go on. It's only a cat. Who's going to mind?"

event: Elsie says the cat hasn't agreed, and she wouldn't anyway; she sits down on the slates.
prose: "He hasn't agreed," Elsie said. She said it at once, quite simply. "He's a cat. He can't agree. So I can't." She thought about it a moment longer, with the sun on her face and the slates warm under her. "And I wouldn't anyway," she said. "Even if he could. Even if it was allowed. He's frightened and cross, and that's his to be, and I'm not going to reach into him and make him something else." Then she let go of Tamsin and sat down where she was, on the slates just below the ridge, tucked her skirt round her knees, and made herself comfortable.

memory.fact: Elsie has never once used her class to make anyone feel anything.

event: Below, Cora stops with her pen above the ledger, then writes.
prose: Far below in the lane, Elsie caught a movement and looked down. It was Cora. She was standing exactly where she had been, with the ledger open on her palm, and her pen had been moving steadily all this time. Now it had stopped. It hung above the page. Cora was looking up at the roof, at Elsie sitting on the slates, and she stood quite still with her pen in the air for a long moment, as if she had heard something she needed to think about. Then she looked down and wrote. It was a short line. She wrote it slowly.

changes.note: Bond: Cora 15 → 20 (saw Elsie refuse to charm the cat with a skill)

event: Elsie holds out the rag and tells Pudding about her plants, humming in between.
prose: Elsie unfolded the rag with the fish paste on it and laid it on her flat palm and held it out, up the slope, toward the cat, not too close. Then she talked to him. She told him about her plants. She told him about Mrs Pennywhistle, who was oldest, and Sunny, who had two lemons coming, and Doris, who wanted very little, and Captain the mint, who smelled nice and would probably interest him a great deal. She told him in a soft ordinary voice, as if the roof were her kitchen. In between, when she ran out of plants, she hummed.

memory.fact: Now and then Elsie hums without knowing it.

event: Pudding comes down the ridge a step at a time and climbs into Elsie's lap.
prose: Pudding looked at her. He looked at the rag. His nose twitched. He looked away over the city as if he had better things to consider, and then back at the rag. Elsie went on humming. After a long while, with great dignity, Pudding stood up on the ridge and came down it toward her, one step, and stopped, and another step, and stopped, his yellow eyes fixed on her face. He sniffed the rag. He ate a little of the paste. Then he stepped off the slates onto Elsie's knees, turned round twice, and lay down in her lap as if it had been his idea.

event: He purrs, and Tamsin sits close behind Elsie on the slates to steady her.
prose: He was heavy and warm and smelled of fish and soot, and after a moment, under Elsie's hand, he began to purr. It was a deep rusty rumbling purr that Elsie could feel through her whole lap. She laughed softly, and stroked him, and he pushed his head up into her hand. The roof tilted under her. She had not noticed how steep it was until she had a cat on her lap and no hands free. Then Tamsin was there, behind her, sitting down close at her back on the slates, one boot braced either side of her, to steady her.

event: Tamsin's chin is by Elsie's shoulder, and Elsie leans back into her without thinking.
prose: Tamsin sat so close behind her that her knees were against Elsie's hips and her chest was against Elsie's back. Her chin came to rest just by Elsie's shoulder, beside her neck, and Elsie could feel her breathing there, warm on her bare skin above the halter tie, and her copper curls tickling Elsie's ear. Elsie leaned back. She leaned right back against Tamsin without thinking about it, into the warmth of her, the way she would lean back against a wall in the sun, and let Tamsin take her weight, with the cat purring in her lap.

event: Something warm and quick comes down the Tether from Tamsin; Elsie puts it down to the height.
prose: Something came down the thread. It came down from Tamsin into Elsie's chest, just under her breastbone: something warm and quick and fluttering, like a bird beating against glass, a rush of it, and then again. Elsie felt it go through her and did not know what it was. It was not the ache of the bite. It was not pain at all. She thought about it, with Tamsin's breath on her neck and Tamsin's heart going hard against her back. It must be the height, she decided. Tamsin was frightened of the height, and being brave about it, and Elsie leaned back into her a little more, to comfort her.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 75 → 80 (held Elsie steady on the roof)

event: They climb down; Tamsin goes first and catches Elsie off the last rung, cat and all.
prose: Getting down was harder than getting up. Elsie went back over the ridges on her bottom with Pudding clutched to her chest in both arms, and Tamsin went in front, backwards, guiding her feet. At the gutter Tamsin swung down onto the ladder first and went down it a few rungs, and Elsie came after her, one-handed, slowly, with the cat. Near the bottom Elsie's boot slipped off the rung. She did not fall. Tamsin had already let go of the ladder and turned, and caught her round the waist, cat and all, and lifted her off the last rung and set her down in the lane.

event: The old woman cries over Pudding and gives them each a sugared bun, eaten in the lane.
prose: The old woman cried. She took Pudding out of Elsie's arms and held him against her shawl and cried into his ginger fur, and Pudding put up with it, purring. Then she went into her house and came out with a plate of sugared buns, warm and sticky, and gave them one each, Cora too, and would not hear of anything else. So they ate them standing in the lane, licking sugar off their fingers, with Pudding watching from the doorstep and the smell of leather all round them. Cora ate hers in small neat bites, looking up at the roofs.

event: Tilly picks ginger hairs off Elsie's skirt one by one, carefully, and goes pink.
prose: Elsie's skirt was covered in ginger hairs. They were all down the front of the sage green, where Pudding had lain, dozens of them, fine and bright. Tilly noticed. She stepped close and began to pick them off, one by one, carefully, between her finger and thumb, frowning in concentration, all down the front of Elsie's skirt over her thighs. It took a long time. Somewhere about the middle, Tilly seemed to notice what she was doing and where her hands were, and went pink, deeper and deeper, and kept on picking anyway, very carefully, and did not look up.

event: At the Tipsy Heron Tamsin pays for stew for herself, Elsie and Tilly, and Cora pays for her own.
prose: At the Tipsy Heron, Tamsin went to the counter first and would not let Elsie near it. "Mine," she said, and bought three bowls of stew, and counted the coppers out of her own purse onto the wood, and carried them back to the table two at a time, one for Elsie and one for Tilly and one for herself. "You fed me rolls and buns and stew all week," she said, when Elsie opened her mouth. "My turn." Cora went to the counter by herself afterward and laid down her own coins for her own bowl, and sat at the end of the table.

changes.note: Tamsin pays three bowls of stew at four pips: 103 → 91 pips

event: Tilly asks Tamsin if the sleeping is the Tether; Elsie says she honestly doesn't know.
prose: Tilly ate quickly, for once, and then sat with her spoon in her hand and her eyes on Tamsin. "Tamsin," she said. "The sleeping. Last night, the whole night through." She looked at Elsie, and back. "Is that the Tether? Is it doing that?" Tamsin looked at Elsie too. They both looked at her. Elsie put down her spoon and thought about it honestly. "I don't know," she said. "I honestly don't. It might be. Or it might be that you were tired out from wolves." She shook her head. "I really don't know, Tilly."

memory.fact: The night after the Tether, Tamsin slept the night through for the first time in a year.

event: Cora says she will write it down if it happens again.
prose: "If it happens again," Cora said from the end of the table, "I'll write it down." They all turned to look at her. She was eating her stew in small neat spoonfuls, and she did not look up. "One night is one night," she said. "Two is a thing to note. Three is a pattern." She took another spoonful. "Tell me if it happens again, Reyes, and I'll write it down, with the date." Tamsin stared at her. Then she grinned. "I'll tell you every morning," she said. "Slept, Warden. Like a stone." Cora's mouth moved very slightly at one corner.

memory.fact: The night after the Tether, Tamsin slept the night through for the first time in a year.

event: Under the tavern noise Tilly asks Elsie if a Tether can hold two people.
prose: The tavern was loud around them, full of noon noise. Under it, Tilly leaned close to Elsie, so close that her shoulder pressed Elsie's, and her braid brushed Elsie's arm. "Elsie," she said, very low, so that only Elsie would hear, with her eyes on her bowl. "Can a Tether hold two people? At once?" She turned her spoon over. "Two different people. I mean. If they wanted. Is that a thing it can do?" She was not looking at Elsie at all. Her ears had gone pink at the tips.

event: Elsie says she supposes so, if the other one wanted it; Tilly goes scarlet into her stew.
prose: Elsie thought about it. "I suppose so," she said. "If the other one wanted it. I don't see why not. It's only a pact. You can have pacts with more than one person." She smiled at Tilly. "I'd have to ask Cora about the Accord, though, and they'd have to say so in front of her, like Tamsin did." Tilly made a small noise. Then she bent her head over her stew and went scarlet: scarlet to her hairline and down her neck into the collar of her blouse, so red that Elsie put a hand on her forehead to check she was not feverish.

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 55 → 60 (asked if a Tether can hold two)

event: At the guild hall the clerk pays the cat notice, and Elsie, Tamsin and Tilly each pocket a third.
prose:
At the guild hall in the early afternoon the clerk took the cat notice, signed by the old woman in a wobbly hand, and stamped it and counted out the pay: two silver lanterns. Elsie asked him to change both into coppers, and he counted twenty pips onto the desk in a little heap. Elsie divided them there with her finger. Seven to Tamsin, seven to Tilly, who had made the paste and stayed on the ground, and six to herself. Tamsin swept hers into her pouch. Tilly tucked hers in her apron. Elsie wished her window open over her six pips, to see.

event: Tilly squeaks as her window opens by itself, and turns it to show Elsie: Level up.
prose:
Tilly squeaked. A window had opened in the air in front of her, all by itself, and she jumped back from it as if it were a wasp. Then she read it, and her mouth fell open, and she grabbed Elsie's arm and turned the window round with her other hand so that Elsie could read it too.

event: Cora says she has her report to write, and goes in at the charcoal door.
prose: Cora closed her ledger with a small exact snap. "I have my report to write," she said, to all three of them, and looked at Elsie as she said it. "The guildmaster will want the cat." She inclined her head, the small bow, and turned, and walked back across the hall through the afternoon crowd to the charcoal-painted door. Elsie watched her go. The whispers had started again round the tables as Cora passed, and Cora walked through them straight-backed, as if she could not hear them. She opened the door and went in.

event: Tamsin says her mother's barge ties up on the Long Cut tomorrow, and asks Elsie to meet her.
prose: Tamsin had been standing with her hands in her pockets and her eyes on the floor. Now she looked up. "Elsie," she said. "My mum's barge ties up on the Long Cut tomorrow. At the coal wharf, by the lock, first thing." She said it fast, to get it out. "She's been down the cut a fortnight, she'll be in for two days, loading. I thought—" She rubbed the back of her neck with her wrapped hand. "You said you'd like to meet her. If you meant it. You don't have to have meant it. People say things."

memory.fact: Tamsin's mother's barge ties up at the Long Cut coal wharf, by the lock, for two days.
Tamsin's mother's barge ties up at the Long Cut coal wharf, by the lock, for two days.
Tamsin's mother's barge ties up at the Long Cut coal wharf, by the lock, for two days.
Tamsin's mother's barge ties up at the Long Cut coal wharf, by the lock, for two days.
Tamsin's mother's barge ties up at the Long Cut coal wharf, by the lock, for two days.

event: Elsie says yes before she has finished, and says she will bring honey cake.
prose: "Yes," Elsie said, before Tamsin had finished. "Yes. Yes, of course I meant it, I'd love to. Tomorrow? First thing? Yes." She took Tamsin's good hand in both of hers. "And I'll bring honey cake," she said. "A whole one. The baker's going to teach me tonight, she said so this morning, I'm going to learn it properly. I'll bake it tonight and bring it in the morning." She beamed up at Tamsin. "Your mother loves honey cake. I'll bring her the best one I can make."

event: Tamsin laughs and says she never told her that; Elsie says she did, and wrote it down.
prose: Tamsin laughed. It burst out of her, surprised and delighted. "Honey cake! Where'd you get that? I never told you that." Elsie looked at her. "You did," she said, quite seriously. "On the canal wall. The day we did the rats. You'd just choked on your bread, and I asked what she liked, and you said honey cake. She likes honey cake." She patted her satchel, where the notebook was. "I wrote it down that night. Under your name. Her mother likes honey cake. And I asked the baker this morning."

memory.fact: Elsie keeps a notebook of the birthdays and favourite things of people she loves.
Elsie keeps a notebook of the birthdays and favourite things of people she loves.

event: Tamsin stops laughing and looks at Elsie as if something hit her.
prose: Tamsin stopped laughing. She stopped all at once, as if Elsie had reached out and pressed a hand flat over her mouth, and she stood there in the middle of the guild hall and looked at Elsie. She looked as if something had hit her: as if she had walked into a door in the dark. Her lips were parted. Her green eyes had gone very wide and very bright, fixed on Elsie's face, and her ears were going red, slowly, and she did not seem to know they were. She did not say anything for a long moment. "You wrote it down," she said at last, hoarse.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 80 → 90 (Elsie wrote down her mother's honey cake)

event: Tilly says she has a brew to finish and goes, then runs back to hug Elsie, then goes.
prose: "I've a brew to finish," Tilly said, "at home, it's been sitting since this morning, and if I leave it any longer it'll go solid, or the other thing." She hugged her apron and turned to go, and went three steps. Then she turned round and ran back and flung her arms round Elsie's neck and hugged her, hard and quick, with her face pressed into Elsie's shoulder for a moment. Then she let go, very pink, and said, "Sorry. Bye. Sorry," and turned and went, properly this time, out through the doors with her braids flying.

event: Tamsin walks Elsie home along Thimble Canal with Margery on her shoulder.
prose: Tamsin walked Elsie home. She did not ask; she swung Margery up onto her shoulder and turned along Thimble Canal when Elsie did, and walked beside her in the afternoon sun, close, with her bandaged arm brushing Elsie's every few steps. The canal was bright and busy, full of boats, and the lanterns hung unlit on their strings. Tamsin was quiet most of the way. Once she looked at Elsie sideways as if to say something, and then did not. Once, at the bridge with the cats, she laughed to herself, low, for no reason Elsie could see.

event: At the Honeycomb door Tamsin says tomorrow, early, and goes off whistling.
prose: At the Honeycomb door Tamsin stopped on the cobbles below the step. "Tomorrow," she said. "Early. I'll come for you here. First light." She grinned, crooked, and shifted Margery on her shoulder. "Bring the cake." Then she turned and went off along the canal path the way they had come, with the great axe over her shoulder, and she was whistling. Elsie stood on the step and watched her go, and listened. Tamsin whistled all the way along Thimble Canal, loud and tuneless and happy, until she turned the corner by the bridge.

event: In the attic Elsie writes: Tamsin's mother, the barge, the Long Cut, honey cake.
prose: The attic was hot under the sloped roof in the middle of the afternoon. Elsie pushed the round window wide and sat on the bed with the notebook on her knees, and turned to the page of names, and found her pencil. Under Tamsin, under Tether and she said leave it, she wrote, in her careful round hand: Her mother. The barge. The Long Cut, the coal wharf, by the lock. Then, on its own line, and underlined: Honey cake. Tomorrow. She looked at the word cake for a while with the pencil against her lip, and felt a little sick, and very happy.

event: She sleeps an hour with the round window open and the canal sounds coming in.
prose: She lay down on the narrow bed on top of the blanket, with the round window open, and the canal sounds came in: water slapping on stone, a boatman calling, someone laughing on a bridge, the creak of the lanterns on their strings. She meant only to rest her eyes. The thread under her breastbone was warm and quiet. She slept a whole hour, deep, with one arm flung over her face and the warm air moving over her from the window, and woke with the light gone gold and slanting across the floor, and the bakery below gone quiet for closing.

event: At closing she comes down with the firewood money, and the baker ties an apron on her.
prose: At six, when the Honeycomb had shut its doors and turned its sign, Elsie came down the stairs with two copper pips in her hand for the firewood and held them out. The baker took them without looking at them and dropped them in the jar on the shelf. Then she took a clean apron off the hook, a big white one, and came round the counter and put it over Elsie's head, and turned her round by the shoulders, and tied it behind her waist herself in a firm double bow. "Sleeves up," the baker said. Elsie, who had no sleeves, peeled off her gloves.

changes.note: Two pips to the baker for the oven's firewood: 113 → 111 pips

memory.fact: The baker lets her lodger use the ovens after closing, for the cost of the firewood.

event: The baker sets a whole comb of honey on the table; Elsie pays for that too, and the baker lets her.
prose: The baker went into the back and came out with a whole comb of honey on a plate, a great slab of it, heavy and gold and dripping, still in its wax, and set it on the table in the middle of the bakery. It smelled of summer. Elsie looked at it, and then reached for her purse. "How much is the honey?" she asked. "I said I'd pay for everything." The baker looked at her a moment, and then said five pips. Elsie gave her a silver lantern, and the baker gave her five coppers back, and let her.

changes.note: Five pips to the baker for a whole comb of honey: 111 → 106 pips
Elsie ends the chapter with 106 pips: 10 lanterns, 6 pips
Tamsin ends the chapter with 98 pips
Tilly ends the chapter with 95 pips

event: The baker says nothing is written down, so watch; Elsie watches every move.
prose: "None of this is written down," the baker said, rolling up her own sleeves. "Not anywhere. Never has been. So you watch." She pointed a floury finger at Elsie's face. "Watch my hands. Not my face, my hands." Elsie watched. She watched every move: how much flour, scooped and levelled with a knife; how many eggs, cracked one-handed; how the butter was cut, and softened, and beaten until it went pale. She watched the way the baker's broad hands moved, without measuring anything, sure and quick, as if the cake were already in them and only needed letting out.

memory.fact: Agnes Merriweather's honey cake is known all along Thimble Canal, and she has never written it down.
Agnes Merriweather's honey cake is known all along Thimble Canal, and she has never written it down.

event: She melts the comb slowly while Elsie stirs and hums, and the baker says hum less.
prose: The baker broke the comb into a pan and set it over the low heat at the back of the oven, and gave Elsie a wooden spoon. "Stir," she said. "Slow. Don't let it catch." Elsie stirred. The honey melted slowly out of the wax, gold into gold, and the whole bakery filled with the smell of it, warm and dark and sweet, and Elsie stirred and stirred and began, without meaning to, to hum. The baker put down her bowl. "Hum less," she said. "You're stirring to the tune. It wants stirring to the honey." Elsie stopped humming, and stirred to the honey.

event: Elsie writes each step in her notebook in a floury pencil, and the baker reads over her shoulder.
prose: She had the notebook open on the corner of the table beside the flour crock, and every time the baker did something new, Elsie stopped and wrote it down with the stub of pencil, quickly, in her careful round hand gone hurried. Melt slow, don't let it catch. Butter till pale. Fold, don't beat, after the flour. The pencil got floury and the pages got floury and there was honey on the corner of one. The baker came and stood behind her and read over her shoulder, breathing through her nose. Once she put out a finger and tapped a line. "More than that," she said. Elsie crossed it out and wrote more.

event: The baker says her own mother taught her, and she has never taught anyone since.
prose: They poured the batter into the round tin together, the baker tipping the bowl and Elsie scraping it out with a spatula, every last bit. The baker set the tin in the oven and shut the door on it, and stood back and wiped her hands on her apron, slowly. She looked at the oven door. "My mother taught me that," she said, quietly, not looking at Elsie. "At this table. When I was younger than you." She was quiet a moment. "I've not had anyone to teach it to since. Not in forty years." Then she turned and began to clear the bowls.

memory.fact: The Honeycomb's baker taught Elsie her honey cake, the first she has taught it in forty years.
The Honeycomb's baker taught Elsie her honey cake, the first she has taught it in forty years.
The Honeycomb's baker taught Elsie her honey cake, the first she has taught it in forty years.

event: The cake comes out golden; the baker covers it with a cloth and says it must rest a night.
prose: At eight the baker opened the oven, and there it was: round and high and golden, dark at the edges, glistening with honey on top, and the smell came out in a great warm wave and filled the bakery to the rafters. Elsie made a small helpless noise. The baker lifted it out with a cloth and turned it onto the rack and looked at it, and nodded once. Then she took a clean white cloth and laid it over the whole cake, gently, and tucked it in round the edges. "It rests a night," she said. "Covered. You don't cut it till morning."

memory.fact: Her honey cake takes a whole comb of honey, and must rest a night under a cloth before it is cut.

event: Elsie asks why; the baker says some things are better for waiting.
prose: "Why?" Elsie asked. She was looking at the shape of the cake under the cloth, round and warm, and wanted very much to look at it again. "Why does it have to rest? It looks finished." The baker smoothed the cloth over the top of it with her broad hand, slowly, the way a person smooths a blanket over someone asleep. "Some things are better for waiting," she said. She said it simply, the way she said everything, as if it were a fact about flour. Then she looked at Elsie a moment, and patted the cloth once, and turned away to the sink.

event: Elsie washes every bowl while the baker sits on a stool and watches her.
prose: Elsie washed every bowl. She washed the honey pan and the mixing bowls and the spoons and the spatula and the tin the butter had come in, and the jug and the flour scoop, at the deep stone sink with her bare arms in the hot water to the elbow. The baker did not help. She sat on her stool by the ovens with her hands folded on her apron and watched Elsie work, the whole time, without saying anything, in the warm dim bakery with the cake resting under its cloth. When Elsie turned round with the last bowl, the baker was smiling.

event: Upstairs Elsie feels Tamsin down the Tether, settled and warm, somewhere across town.
prose: Upstairs, in the warm dark of the attic, Elsie sat on the edge of the bed and felt for the thread. It was there, under her breastbone, running out through the round window and away across the city toward the docks, warm and steady. At the far end of it, Tamsin. The ache in the forearm was still there, but faint now, hardly anything. And under it something else, quiet and settled and warm, like a fire banked for the night. Tamsin was at rest, somewhere across town. Elsie sat with her hand flat on her chest a long while, feeling it.

event: She writes her weekly letter to her mother: a cat, a cake, and a girl who sleeps now.
prose: Then she lit the candle and got out her paper and pen and wrote her weekly letter to her mother. Dear Mum, she wrote. I'm level two now, and I'll explain that properly another time. Today we got a cat named Pudding down off a roof without any skills at all, only fish paste and talking to him about the plants. Tonight the baker taught me to make her honey cake, which lives in her hands, and it is resting under a cloth downstairs. And my friend Tamsin, who used to wake up in the night, sleeps now. She wrote three pages.

memory.fact: Elsie writes her mother a letter every week.

event: She sets her boots by the door for the morning, and goes to bed early.
prose: When the letter was folded and addressed, Elsie set her boots side by side by the door, where she would find them at first light without fumbling: laced loose, ready to pull on, toes to the door. She laid the satchel beside them with the notebook in it, and the clean cloth the baker had given her for wrapping the cake folded on top. Then she pinched out the candle and got into bed while the sky in the round window was still blue, and pulled the blanket up, with her hand on her chest over the thread.
